text:
Ideas for crescendo besides just “getting louder”

I just a quick share if you’re finding your dynamics a bit boring or constrained. The problem with “just getting louder” is you run out of room really quickly.

A couple motivating examples:

1. Suppose you have several phrases you need to chain together. Each phrase has a little crescendo to it. You want to make it feel as though the whole passage is building to something bigger and not sound repetitive.

2. You play a chord say at a ”pp” the next chord is supposed to crescendo but still quiet at a “p”. This is incredibly hard to do without either sounding the same or overshooting it.

Here are some ideas:

\* Layering. This is where you gradually bring in more of the accompaniment as you crescendo.

\* Pedal. Consider how holding the pedal a little bit longer and a little bit shorter will change the feeling.

\* Articulation. If you use a detached articulation into a more legato articulation, you can give the feeling of building into something and vice versa.

\* Time. When you choose to use rubato or NOT use rubato you can create moments of surprise.

Let’s take a look at how these ideas work in our examples. 

Layering:

\* In Example 1, play the accompaniment quietly in the first phrase, and gradually bring it in more and more by the last phrase the accompaniment is booming as the melody line soars over it. The effect is one tremendous climax as opposed to a repetitive phrasing.

\* In Example 2, consider your first chord you play quietly. The second time you play the chord EXACTLY the same, but you bring out only the top note a bit more. This gives you a feeling of quiet but louder.

This is the power of layering.

Pedaling:

\* In Example 1, let us start with very short pedals. Frequent repedaling. Maybe even certain parts are completely dry. Then you sustain pedal a little bit longer. By the final phrase, we hold the pedal for entire measure for example. Even slightly dissonant contributes to the effect. Now the audience is feeling a huge rush as you reach the peak.

\* In Example 2, we release pedal early for the chord and as we crescendo we hold pedal a little bit longer, and longer, and we give the effect of crescendo without necessarily actually getting much louder.

Time:

\* For example 1, we work against the idea of rubato. As we crescendo, we can build quite loudly. The audience will expect a rubato heading into climax. But we withhold the rubato. We DO NOT rubato even as we climb higher. The audience is now sitting on the edge of their seat. When we finally do rubato, now they are just completely in our hands, the climax will feel incredibly emotional.

\* For example 2, we also use rubato and NO rubato to control the effect. Conventional wisdom says as a chord is held the sound decays so the next chord should come in and match the sound level. We can subvert this expectation! So we if we let time decay and NOT match the lower sound level, it will actually sound tense and that will feel like a crescendo is happening even if you are simply playing with time.

This post is getting long so I will leave it as an exercise how you can use articulation to create the effect of a crescendo without actually getting louder!

I built a piano fingering visualizator

Hello, it´s my first time in this subreddit!

I like playing piano, i´m no expert; but I really enjoy it. However, I´m a little more experienced in programming :)

The thing is, I wanted to learn a specific piece, but I found it rather hard to find tutorial videos that include hands and fingering. I´m learning piano with a teacher, so it is easier for me to learn when I can see hand motions and positions.

Soooo.... I started **OpenNote** as a fun open-source project, to learn the fundamentals of model training. I´m aware that there has been more fingering software before (most notably, Concert Pianist), but my benchmarks show my custom model ¨helios¨ achieves the highest score across all piano fingering datasets (i.e. PIG, Thumbset, etc.).

About the model, i trained it on aproximately 10K videos of overhead piano covers, and the already existing rulesets (Ramoneda, Parncutt...)

About the UI and appearance, I tried to make it similar to popular piano tutorials on Youtube, including cool note and skin shaders. I´m also testing out a feature in which the user inputs any Youtube link of a piano cover / audio, and the program transcribes it to MIDI for the fingering calculator to play.

![img](qlojtj4aaiwh1 "try it out! :)")

**I am aware the ¨learning¨ aspect of the program needs some work, as the app has, or at least i consider, it does, a lot of potential as a standalone piano learning app. I´m actively working on making the general experience feel more like a lesson than just playback.**

I would appreciate if you could try it out and give me your feedback as musicians! The fingering might not be perfect, it even gets somewhat cursed sometimes... I´m working on it! I will greatly value your suggestions as pianists for hopefully improving the finger accuracy.

text:
Digital vs Acoustic

Don't get me wrong. I'm really a noob and learn by applying what I read and see in books/online and play for fun in massive time intervals. I had some lessons, maybe 10 in total, 8 or so years ago? Yet, while they gave me an idea of what to practice, it never really was revolutionary or provided much of a feedback, other than listening to what I prepared/practiced.

What I want to say is: After having practiced a song that I really love for about a week now on the digital piano at home, I wanted to try playing it on an acoustic.

So I went to this place that I know of, which has rental rooms with acoustic pianos in them. It's nothing special, very cheap compared to the "official" places, but the pianos are really really not in the best shape. Keys feel stuck/sticky, overly heavy, imbalanced, unsettled, clunky, require imho more initial force than they should for the hammer to mobe, can't be trusted.

But still, it's an acoustic.

It turned out to be a massive reminder for me, for how loud the left hand can be on an acoustic, compared to the perfect vst with the just right piano I like and the pianos volume being turned down, if you aren't super graceful.

It showed me how tense I am and how much more relaxed I need to be "in a different way" than on a digital piano.

Not that I don't like/appreciate the digital piano.

Then came back home after 1h on the acoustic and I had such a better time with my left hand sounding so much more like an accompaniment, because I had to be so extremely relaxed to not completely swallow whatever the right hand is playing with the left hand.

Anyway, I'm happy I could play an acoustic again, although I really disliked the feeling of that particular piano.

I've never played on an expensive acoustic piano, so I can't really tell how that would feel.

I just know the weight is way more dynamically controllable, compared to the digital piano.

I'm sure a properly maintained and generally a piano in a better state is going to be worlds ahead than whatever that was, but still, it was nice.

text:
Spotify's Burgmüller Op. 100 recording (Donatello Renando) seems to have a lot of deviations/mistakes from the IMSLP score. Am I hearing this right?

I'm a piano teacher and just assigned my student the first two etudes from Burgmüller's Op. 100. To prepare, I played through them myself to find the trouble spots he might hit. I then put on a full-playlist recording of the set on Spotify (Donatello Renando) and noticed a bunch of very obvious discrepancies right away.

I'm following the 25 Etudes, Op. 100 edition from IMSLP. Here's what I've caught so far, through Etude 4:

No. 1

Left hand plays quarter notes where the score has whole notes.

In m. 15, 18, and 20, he plays staccato eighth notes in the left hand instead of half notes.

No. 2

Pedal goes down in m. 7.

Plays an F in the right hand instead of a G in m. 9.

Plays a D♯ in m. 19, but it belongs in m. 18.

Slur is missing in m. 25.

M. 27 is played in both the first and second endings, but it should only be played in the first.

The final fermata is barely held.

No. 3 (more subtle)

In mm. 12 and 14, he seems to add a brief A in the left hand between the G and B on the dotted half notes.

In m. 27 (third to last measure), he seems to add a C in the left hand on the first chord, creating a small clash/cluster.

No. 4

Mm. 5-6 are rushed, with the quarter rests squeezed when they should be open and marcato.

In m. 16, the move to the quarter-note B and D goes up a step to C and E. That throws off beats 3-4 of that measure and beats 1-2 of the next.

Two measures later, the same right-hand figure appears and he plays the correct B and D.

I couldn't find anything blatant in Nos. 5 and 6, and that's as far as I've listened.

I can't tell whether these are sloppy takes that slipped through, deliberate "spot the error" quirks, or something else. The blatant left-hand rhythm changes and the repeated m. 27 across both endings seem too obvious to be simple slips.

A few questions:

Has anyone else listened to this recording and noticed the same things?

Is there a different Op. 100 edition where these differences would actually be in the score?

Any recommendations for a clean, reliable recording I can point my students toward?
label: question

text:
Help with Saint-Saëns PC2 opening cadenza?

Hello, 

I'm starting to work on the opening of Saint-Saëns 2nd concerto and I would love some outside ("pro") opinion on the fingering of a specific pattern. 

I have no problem with the initial upward movement. Both hand finally land a diminished 5th appart (A - Eb) and start a parallel scale downward: still no issue. My problem is with the broken diminished seventh arpeggios, zigzagging all the way down the keyboard a sixth appart.

The isolated pattern goes:

RH:  Eb-F# C-Eb   A-C   F#-A Eb...

LH:  F#-A   Eb-F# C-Eb A-C   F#...

For the right hand, my fingering for the above is 23 14 15 34, and I'm pretty quite happy with that. I didn't have to look for it, it literally jumped at me.

The left hand is where I was a doubt. If I play left-hand alone, the "right" fingering for me is 32 41 32 51. It's very fluid that way.

BUT, when I bring hands together, the left hand always goes to 32 41 32 ***41*** 32 41 32 ***41***. The 5 gets replaced by a 4. It works too, but I know/feel the other one, with the 5, is more efficient, more elegant, more relaxed for my hand. I think the 4 gets in there because on the right hand we have "34", and the 4 fingers on each hand must be somehow connected. Especially since the whole pattern also has 2 mirror occurences (23 againts 32, 14 against 41)

So, that's not a terrible issue. I think 32 41 32 41 can work at tempo. But it grates on me, I have a feeling the other one (32 41 32 51) is intrinsically better and the very fact that the right hand makes good use of 51 to reposition makes me think the left hand ought to do so as well. And I'm afraid this "hidden connection" between mirrored fingers is a false friend and will come to bite me later on.

I've been working on this for 30" and I'm at a point where I can do both at a slow pace but I still need to focus to stick in the 5. What do you think? Should I let go and let it be with 4 (I'm ready to bring the tempo up), or should I persist on slow practive until the 5 soaks in?

Thanks for reading, and sorry for the long and very specific rant :)

I transposed Christian Schäfer’s Sight Reading Exercises (Op. 45) into all 12 keys and wanted to share the PDFs here for free

It always annoyed me with most sight-reading and method books that beginner pieces are almost exclusively in C, G, or F. By the time a book actually introduces keys like B major, F# major, or Db major, the pieces themselves often have become too hard for sight-reading practice. In my opinion there is not enough simple material in keys with lots of sharps or flats.

I took Christian Schäfer’s (his original name was Arnold Sartorio) Op. 45 sight-reading exercises and re-engraved it, putting every piece through all 12 keys.

I uploaded all 12 volumes (and a single ZIP with everything) to my blog. It’s completely free, no email sign-up or paywall, just direct PDF links: [https://musikkapital.de/schaefers-sight-reading-exercises-transposed-in-all-keys/](https://musikkapital.de/schaefers-sight-reading-exercises-transposed-in-all-keys/)

Also, a follow-up question: do you think one should practice every single day?

Some people recommend taking one day off per week—meaning without touching the piano—to let your hands rest and keep your mind fresh. Would you recommend taking one day off from the piano each week, or should one practice every single day?

text:
[AAP] 2/48: Fugue + pop + sonata form = ??? Here’s my attempt, the first fugue in a cycle. Would love your thoughts

So I've started a cycle of preludes and fugues. My dream for this cycle is to have it played by a great pianist (Víkingur Ólafsson would be nice), for it to be something for fans of the WTC to add to their playlists, and to give fugue-loving pianists something new to play.

When I mention that I want to write fugues, an objection I have heard is: "What can you possibly do that is new? Bach has already done everything there is to do with the fugue."

Where some see a finished form, I see territory he never had the chance to explore. This fugue is a case in point. Modern fugues are often thought of as academic exercises, but what if we fuse a fugue with a pop chord progression, pepper it with little hooks like a pop production, and give it a sonata-form-like recapitulation and coda?

The accompanying video demonstrates many of the ideas realized in this fugue. The subject was built around I-IV-V with the idea that it could be repeated like a pop song; the song uses it to build into the climax by taking it away. Pop producers are masters at filling every moment with little hooks like ear candy, and I've attempted to do that here, increasing their frequency throughout, until towards the end where every voice seems to be nonstop hooks. In the "recap" (1:44 in the video), the subject re-enters in the same voices and tones as in the exposition, but with a new arrangement, leading into a coda (2:14 in the video) with new material, 3-voice stretto, and development of a figure from the answer. There are plenty more details for you to discover.

Some of you will hear a lesser Bach, and that’s a comparison I can’t win. I’d ask you to try hearing it as something else: a fugue with a melody that has subtle, modern influences, an approach that is both reminiscent of Bach yet something novel. I hope you will find ideas that maybe challenge the premise that there is nothing new left to do with the fugue and that it's possible to write a new fugue that's more than an academic exercise, something with a great melody and fun to listen to.

So what do you think of injecting pop and sonata-form into the fugue? And what are some other ways we might be able to evolve the fugue as a genre and potentially grow its audience?

text:
Which collection would you learn A to Z?

Over your lifetime as a pianist, which collection would you want to learn in its entirety? Would you even consider doing this in the first place?

For example, quite a few people learn the whole Chopin Etudes, or Beethoven sonatas. Has anyone on here done this? I'm not talking about learning only this one work in one go and nothing else, but learning it over a couple of years and keeping it as something to study over and over.

I'll go first. Collections I'm interested in (in order):

* Chopin Etudes
* Bach WTC
* Liszt Transcendental Etudes
* Debussy Preludes
* Beethoven sonatas

I'm quite drawn to Chopin Etudes for some reason. I think I just like figuring out the different techniques, and some are among my favourite Chopin pieces from a pure musical perspective (25/12, 25/5, 25/1, 10/9).

I'm reading through the whole WTC bit by bit. I've finished reading through book 1, and now I'm using it for warming up for my evening practice. I tend to spend some time on specific preludes and sometimes fugues, so I'll probably learn them all eventually. Plus is fascinating.

Liszt TEs are probably my second pick after Chopin's. The problem is how hard they are. I'm not entirely sure I'll ever be able to even get the hardest ones up to 80% or 90% polish, most likely not. And I'm not a big fan of all of them (no. 1 huh). But there's something about this work that's got a legendary aura and some of these etudes are peak music (no. 11 is my favourite).

Debussy Preludes are also very very interesting to me. There's so much variety in them, and they aren't as hard technically as other collections. I'll probably read through all of them as well and maybe work on about at least half of them over time.

The last one is... tricky. So many people love all Beethoven sonatas, but I don't really see the appeal. Some of them are among my favourite pieces of all times, but some others are quite meh (I dropped Op. 10 no. 3 this year, I just didn't enjoy the first movement to put in the work). I might read through all of them slowly, but I doubt I'll ever try to properly learn them all.

There are so many other good choices. Mozart or Haydn sonatas, Scarlatti sonatas (I'm also reading through all of them, one a day, I'm at K179), Scriabin sonatas (this would be really hard plus I don't like no. 4 and no. 1), etc.

**My personal pick would be Chopin Etudes**. I think I could spend a lifetime on this and not get bored. I'd pick Liszt TEs second if it wasn't for its difficulty, so I suppose I'd pick the WTC (also difficult but in a different way).

What's yours? Is there any book or collection you love and have fully learnt or are planning to? Ideally around 1h or longer (aka. not something short like Brahms op. 117).

I'm secretly hoping that someone will say "all Czerny etudes" :D

text:
Can I play in the Chopin Competition?

I find there’s a lot of people who ask this who receive very harsh responses, saying it’s virtually impossible. I understand this might be true for the average person but I was under the impression there are a lot of not-so-average pianists in this sub reddit. Most comments will say “if you aren’t a prodigy from birth it’s impossible” or “if you haven’t won a million competitions it’s impossible”. To that I say, screw them! 

My favorite example is Lucas DeBargue. He only started taking piano seriously at about 21 and took home 4th at the Tchaikovsky competition 4 years later. If you invest all your time and energy into the instrument with the guidance of a world renowned teacher (of which there are more then you’d expect—ready and willing to help) anything is possible!

Out of all the people who say it’s impossible, I doubt many are conservatory trained. The amount of elitism I’ve seen coming from this subreddit, especially from people who aren’t professionals, is ridiculous. I know many incredible pianists who were good from a young age, but in now way prodigies—but maybe people who aren’t in the competition circuit have a lower standard of what makes a prodigy. Most people I’ve met in international competitions were not playing chopin etudes in elementary school. 

Maybe I’m saying this as a cope (as someone who started late but hopes to place in the Chopin competition someday) but I think people on this sub put competition winners on such a pedestal that we forget they kinda are just normal people at the end of it.

 This is just from my perspective as someone who’s been in the high end youth competition circuit for a while, but what do you guys think?

text:
How do you handle positive feedback from your teachers?

I started taking piano lessons again about 7 weeks ago after a 12 years long break. 

I played piano during my high school years and then stopped just to start playing and taking lessons again at the end of August/beginning of September. 

My teacher is an international concert pianist, she is so incredibly good I seriously look up to her with the upmost awe and respect wanting to absorb everything that she is willing to teach me becuase if it can make me even a fraction as good as her, I’ll consider it a huge win. 

One thing that I am not used to receiving as a piano student, is positive feedback. I’ve had several piano teachers during my teenage years and praise was something so rare from them that I guess I never got used to receiving it. 

Today my current teacher had me play Liszt consolation No.2 something that I’ve been working on with her for the last 6 weeks and that I had already learned 15 years ago so wasn’t really learning from zero. 

The piano I take lessons on is on a small stage in a place where concerts with small audiences can be held so there were chairs set out in the room for a concert this weekend. 

My teacher sat front row and had me practice performing the piece for her (I have severe performance anxiety).

While I was playing for her I was internally freaking out because I didn’t feel grounded and in control. I felt like no matter how much I tried, I couldn’t put weight in my arms and felt like they wanted to float away from the piano (I’m not exaggerating).

I managed to get through the piece and when I was done playing it she immediately told me that she liked all of it. That she found my interpretation very interesting and personal. She liked what I had to say through my playing and how I said it. That my playing held her attention and spiked engaged interest throughout the entire piece in a way that genuinely made her wonder what would happen next and that it always followed with pleasant surprise at my musical choices. She also said that my timing felt natural and musically convincing and she never felt awkward rests or pauses. That everything flowed together beautifully and that I told a beautiful story. 

🫠 I didn’t even know how to act when she told me all this I was so taken aback.

It’s not the first time she tells me she likes how I tell a story while playing it. I never know how to act when she tells me this but this time she added all these other comments about my playing and I forgot how to human for a second. Like, how am I supposed to act, what am I supposed to think? What am I supposed to say? 

Like for real I don’t even know what to make of all this feedback. How am I supposed to use it? What do it do with it? 

I also feel like my mind is playing tricks. Did she really mean it? If so, what does it mean? She was just trying to be encouraging. Was she? 

How can my experience and her experience of the same piece be so different? Am I not listening to my own music? 

I end up convincing myself that nothing she said is true. And if it is true, it’s not something remarkable or that I should feel proud of becuase literally anyone can play Liszt’s consolation better than me anyways. Plus there is so much I still have to improve so I cannot accept this positive feedback as true. 

Then I look at myself and realize I’m acting like a crazy person just because my teacher said something nice and I don’t know how to freaking handle it. What is wrong with me🫠😂
label: experience

text:
Finally got unstuck from measures 15-16 of Alla Turca

Didn't play piano for about 15 years. Played for about 10 years on and off as a pre-teen/young adult. I started begging for a piano at 8 years old and finally got one at 11. Sadly I sold my piano during a bad marriage in my early twenties and didn't play again since then until earlier this year. Because I was self-taught I didn't really have very much real knowledge to fall back on except for my amazing high school music teacher which taught me how to read music. I read it far too slowly to be able to play piano while reading but being able to read it did give me a better understanding of music and piano (her instrument of choice as well). 

So what did I do when returning to piano after 15 years? I made the maybe not so smart decision to learn Alla Turca. It started with my 9-year-old who wanted to learn to play piano so I began to teach him and he absolutely fell in love with Alla Turca. He started trying to sound it out on his own. It inspired me to learn it. I had learned a simplified version when I was a child thanks to my Yamaha keyboard. This time I studied professionals playing for hours and paid attention to their exact finger placement. 

I breezed through learning measures 1 through 14 and even got the speed down. Not perfect by any means but not slow either. But measure 15 and 16 have haunted me for about 2 months 😅 I felt like when I played it was the same as when you first learn a tongue twister and you can't get it right even though you know the words. 

  
But I finally have it, my brain has finally connected the pieces and I can finally play those two measures and at a fair pace, improvement certainly needed lol I can play almost at speed with a high chance of small mistakes or half speed with little to no mistakes so I'm getting there. 

I knew going into it that this would take me a really really long time to learn. And I know that even after I learn it I still have a lot more to learn to perfect it. I'm okay with that in fact I've really been enjoying it. Even if measures 15 and 16 really kicked my butt 😂 

I don't know any piano lovers anymore so I just had to share this with someone somewhere who would understand my joy. The joy of playing and the joy of seeing the same love for piano I had as a child in the eyes of my own child.

text:
Getting better at sight reading piano: answers to the questions I see most

**TL;DR:** Little and often (5-15 minutes most days) beats long, rare sessions. Use music a grade or two below your level, keep it fun, and find ways to check your mistakes. Free resources below. App plug at the very end, clearly labelled!

\--

I see a lot of posts on this subreddit (and others) about learning to read music. The same questions come up again and again:

* How can I get better at sight reading?
* What should my practice routine look like?
* What pieces should I play?
* Why is sight reading so difficult, especially on piano?
* Are alternatives like Synthesia, watching videos or writing in note names a decent substitute?

I’d like to try to answer all of them.

What qualifies me? I’m far from the world’s greatest sight reader, but I’ve helped over 1,000 people improve their piano reading through my app, SightReader (more on that at the end). I’ve seen what works in my own data, and I’ve spent a lot of time learning about the science of memory and practice. If you read only one book on the subject, make it [*Learn Faster, Perform Better* by Molly Gebrian](https://www.mollygebrian.com/music-and-the-brain).



**Why is sight reading difficult?**

Probably because you haven’t practised enough for it to be easy yet!

Reading text is difficult too when you start. The difference is that most of us did a huge amount of it as children, so by adulthood it feels trivial. Even then, adults vary widely in reading and comprehension ability.

Music is similar, except far fewer of us lock it in during childhood.



**Why is piano especially hard?**

Piano has a strong claim to being the hardest instrument to sight read. Many instruments are monophonic, meaning they play one note at a time. Other polyphonic instruments (which can play chords) usually can’t play as many notes at once.

On piano, you’re reading two staves, with the possibility of 8-10 note chords. Few instruments (the organ, maybe?) are more demanding.



**Why traditional notation and not an alternative?**

The YouTuber Tantacrul, who works on MuseScore, made [an excellent video on the history of music notation](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=Eq3bUFgEcb4).

Standard notation has its flaws, but there’s a reason most of the world has converged on it: it’s very good at communicating how to play music. And even if some alternatives are good, standard notation is dominant, so it’s the most reliable way to learn new pieces.

Synthesia-style videos are undoubtedly cool and make a great backdrop for watching people play. But a beginner who learns purely that way is at a big disadvantage, both in how easily they pick up new music and in how much music they can discover. The same goes for learning from videos or other methods.



**What about musician X who can’t read music?**

There have always been great musicians, particularly outside classical music, who reportedly can’t read music, from The Beatles to Hans Zimmer. But it’s like the entrepreneurs who dropped out of college (Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, etc.): it worked for them, but that doesn’t make it the best strategy for most people. And most successful musicians can read music to some degree.



**What’s the best practice routine?**

The one you’ll stick to.

Generally, humans learn best with breaks and sleep. That means 10 minutes of sight reading a day beats a single one-hour session per week. Sleep in particular helps the brain lock in new information, which is why daily practice is so effective.

To be clear, more practice is still better: an hour a day beats 10 minutes a day. But an overly ambitious goal you never stick to is worse than an achievable one you actually do. So 5-15 minutes most days is a great starting point for most players.

There are also nuances in how you practise and when you take breaks. For those, I’ll point you to *Learn Faster, Perform Better* again.



**What makes sight reading practice difficult?**

Besides sticking to a routine, I see three main challenges, which hit beginner-to-intermediate players hardest:

1. **Finding new material.** You get diminishing returns from replaying a piece as you start to memorise it, so you need lots of level-appropriate music, which is hard to find as a beginner. (The more advanced you get, the more pieces become playable!)
2. **It’s boring.** You’re playing music well below your level without the satisfaction of mastering a piece, and at earlier levels the music often isn’t that interesting. It’s the learning equivalent of eating your greens!
3. **It’s hard to spot your mistakes.** Especially when you’re new, it’s hard to mark your own homework and know whether you’re playing correctly. A teacher helps, but for most of us that’s one lesson a week, and there are six other days to practise.



**The solution**

Here’s what I’d suggest for each problem:

1. **Finding new material.** Aim for music noticeably easier than what you can play with practice. A good rule of thumb is a grade or two below your current level. Some good sources: Charity shops and second-hand bookshops are also great for cheap piles of music you’ve never seen.
   * [Christian Schäfer’s *Sight Reading Exercises*, Op. 45](https://musescore.com/worldwideweary/schafer-sartorio-sight-reading-exercises-volume1?srsltid=AU7gw4XJMRWqi3W4qaEn4Pz_50IpocCIu8e5QZXBiEXAYO-gdglAFojc) (actually Arnoldo Sartorio under a pseudonym). They start very simple and build up step by step, and they’re free on IMSLP. This is my top recommendation.
   * Graded sight-reading books, like [Paul Harris’s *Improve Your Sight-Reading!* series](https://www.paulharristeaching.co.uk/blog/2017/10/26/how-to-improve-your-sight-reading)
   * Specimen sight-reading tests from exam boards like ABRSM or Trinity
   * Old method books, hymnals and easy collections (Bartók’s *Mikrokosmos*, Burgmüller, Czerny)
   * IMSLP generally, which has a huge library of free, public domain scores
2. **It’s boring.** Make it a game. Track a streak, reward yourself after a week of practice, or set a target number of new pieces per month. Mix in music you actually like: pop arrangements, film music, jazz lead sheets. Playing duets with a friend is also brilliant practice, because the music doesn’t stop when you make a mistake.
3. **It’s hard to spot your mistakes.** Record yourself and listen back with the score in front of you. Mistakes you didn’t notice while playing are often obvious on playback. You can also enter a few bars into free notation software like MuseScore to hear how they should sound. And if you have a teacher, bring them a sight-reading piece now and then rather than only your repertoire.

A few general habits help too: play slowly enough that you rarely stop, keep going when you make a mistake, keep your eyes on the page and try to read a beat or two ahead.



**Full disclosure, self-promotion ahead.** if you’d rather have some of this done for you, this is where my app comes in:

I built [SightReader](https://sightreader.app/) as an adult learner struggling to read piano music, with exactly these problems in mind. You connect a MIDI keyboard (or use microphone mode) and get live feedback on your playing, so you always know whether you got it right. There are lots of ways to practise: from recognising individual notes and chords, to guided lessons, to classic studies (Schäfer is the first one!). It also tracks streaks, so it handles the “make it a game” part too. It’s helped me improve a lot, and over 1,000 other players as well.



You absolutely don’t need an app to learn. Everything above works with a pile of books and some discipline. But if you found this post useful, I hope you’ll forgive the cheeky plug. Happy to answer questions in the comments!

text:
Never found a piano in music schools or public spots, but stumbled upon one drunk at 3 AM in a night club bathroom corridor (Playing Chopin’s Fantaisie-Impromptu)

Hey everyone,

I wanted to share a pretty surreal story that happened to me last night, and I figured if anyone would appreciate the irony, it’s this community.

Exactly one year ago, I decided to learn piano completely from scratch. I didn’t have a teacher, and I didn't really have a traditional goal like passing grades or playing concerts. I write orchestral music, so I originally picked up a 61-key MIDI keyboard purely as a catalyst for my composition and creative process.

However, playing standard plastic synth keys made me fall in love with the instrument itself, and I developed this huge dream: I just wanted to feel and play a real, acoustic piano.

The problem? Acoustic pianos are surprisingly hard to come by where I’ve lived. In my entire life, I had only touched a real piano once—at the train station in Lviv, Ukraine. Recently, I moved to Košice, Slovakia. I searched everywhere—asking around, checking public spots, looking for open spaces or venues—and I literally couldn't find a single accessible acoustic piano anywhere in the city.

Over this past year on my MIDI keyboard, I’ve been teaching myself Chopin’s Fantaisie-Impromptu (Op. 66). It’s been a tough journey, and I always wondered: How would this piece actually feel under my fingers on heavy, weighted acoustic keys? Would I even be able to play it?

Fast forward to yesterday. It was my friend’s birthday, so a group of us went out drinking. We started at an apartment and eventually moved to a night club. At one point during the night, I went to use the restroom.

I turned into the corridor leading to the toilets, and right there—standing aimlessly against the wall with its lid closed—was a real piano.

Out of all the places in the city! I searched music setups, public halls, and cultural spots for months with zero luck, only to find an abandoned acoustic piano outside a nightclub bathroom while intoxicated.

I was so drunk at that moment that I could barely distinguish left from right. But the urge was too strong. I opened the fallboard, sat down, and my friend (the birthday guy) pulled out his phone to film.

Despite my state, the motor memory kicked in, and I managed to pull off a few recognizable sections of Fantaisie-Impromptu. The key action felt completely wild compared to my light MIDI keys, especially given my impaired senses, so the experience was definitely subjective—but pulling those dynamic acoustic notes out of a physical instrument felt incredible.

Just wanted to drop this story here to show that life has a weird sense of humor. Keep practicing, even if your next venue turns out to be a club hallway!

text:
Is classical virtuoso composition dead? My take on Liszt's Galop in A Minor + writing modern virtuoso piano music.

Hi everyone,

​I recently recorded Franz Liszt’s underrated Galop in A Minor S.218:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c\_VjxQ9Anv8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c_VjxQ9Anv8)

​Playing, practicing, and performing this piece made me reflect a lot on the current landscape of piano music and repertoire.

​It feels like today, most contemporary piano composition has heavily leaned towards extreme minimalism. While minimalism certainly has its place and purpose, as a pianist I personally miss the physical energy, the dramatic flair, chromaticism, and unapologetic virtuosity of late Romantic and early 20th-century repertoire.

text:
I made Jamphony, a site where you can jam with others through MIDI piano

Hi everyone,

I've spent a lot of time on multiplayer piano/MIDI sites like PianoRhythm, MultiplayerPiano, Pianoverse, and MultiplayerOrchestra. They are great fun, but I feel they fall short because people almost always end up playing AT each other instead of playing WITH each other.

I made [Jamphony ](https://jamphony.com)to try and fix that and encourage jamming. It supports your MIDI controllers, note input from your computer keyboard, and you can click notes with your mouse.

Rooms are designed to hopefully avoid a free for all situation. There are a limited number of seats so if you're spectating and there is an open seat, you can sit down pick from piano and orchestra instruments. Room hosts can limit how many players can use a specific sound at once. You could limit the room to only two instruments per player for example, so then 5 people won't be on Marimba. If a sound you want is taken, there's a button to request an instrument swap with another seated player.

Also to help people play together, we calculate the chord you are currently playing from your notes and display it on screen to help others follow. Hosts can also use the Next Chord feature, which uses reserved keys they can press to shape out a chord and help direct the rest of the room to it in a progression.

I also wanted to deal with the spam players that usually plague the other sites. Every user has a "reputation" on their profile based on thumbs up/down from other players. As a room host, you can set a min reputation needed to sit down (unless you invite them on purpose). Guests who haven't logged in can still chat and play, but hosts can choose to disable that from their rooms if wanted.

The site launched recently so I'm mostly looking for testing and feedback right now. If you decide to make an account, you can leave feedback for me directly through the settings menu, or dropping feedback in this comments is good too! I am also very interested in hearing feature ideas or improvements to existing features.

Link: [https://jamphony.com](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fjamphony.com)

Thanks!

First-time impressionist piece

My teacher \*really\* wants my next piece to be by one of the impressionists, which is a genre of music that I really don't care for--I find most pieces to be just barely tolerable and nonmelodic. 

My preference is for music from the Romantic era. For context, the pieces I'm currently working on are Beethoven Bagatelle op 33 (all 7 pieces), Chopin Waltz in Am Op 11, and Mendelssohn Venetian Gondola Song, Op 30  #6. I'm currently memorizing and polishing the Chopin and polishing the Mendelssohn. The Beethoven is still in progress and I will probably be working on it for the next 9 mo - year (#3 is polished and memorized, #1 still needs a little work in a couple of measures, and I just started #2). I usually work on one piece that's a bit on the easier side but has some element I need to improve or master (right now, that's the Chopin), one that is right at my current level (the Mendelssohn and #2 of the bagatelles), and one that is a little bit of a stretch (#1 of the bagatelles). My preferences for next pieces would be another Chopin waltz, a mazurka, or a nocturen, and a work by Chaminade (I've fallen in love with Pecheurs de nuit, which would be my stretch piece).

I'm looking for suggestions for pieces that will challenge me but that I'll enjoy musically. (I'm 66, and while I am not "set in my ways," at this point, I know what I do and don't enjoy. If I could find Spanish Renaissance music adapted to piano, I would seriously prefer that as a break from Romantic over Impressionist!)  I'm considering relearning Debussy's Reverie, which I played something like 45 years ago when I was studying seriously in high school, and I also like his Claire de Lune and Satie's Je te Veux, but both of those are in some variant of 3/4 time, and I realize that EVERYTHING, I've been playing has been in either 6/8, 3/8, or 3/4, so a change to 4/4 or 2/4 would be nice. Any additional suggestions would be much appreciated! Also, I have small hands -- I can just barely manage an octave stretch.
